Running title: Regression to the mean in epilepsy trials
Manuscript counts: abstract 207 words; main text 1809 words; 18 references; 2 figures; 1 table. Supplementary tables supplied separately.

Purpose: Regression to the mean (RTM) can resemble improvement in epilepsy trials without treatment. We examined transient rate changes, eligibility selection and detector errors, distinguishing observed RTM from measurement-only Type 3 RTM.

Methods: We reused 1,000,000 simulated 36-month seizure histories. Each condition selected its first eligible two-month baseline and following three-month test period. We varied a transient rate change, the entry threshold, sensitivity and false alarms. Type 3 required RTM on corrected measured counts but not true counts for the same participant and window. Both classifications used a finite true-count reference, scaled by sensitivity for measured counts.

Results: With perfect detection, 64.9% were eligible, 53.8% met observed RTM and median seizure-frequency reduction was 26.7%. Transient rate changes and a higher entry threshold yielded 58.3% and 57.9% observed RTM. At 70% sensitivity, observed RTM was 59.0% and Type 3 affected 7.7% of eligible participants. At one false alarm/day, corresponding values were 69.9% and 41.6%; Type 3 represented 59.4% of measured RTM cases.

Conclusion: Detector errors changed both enrollment and measured trajectories. Measurement-only Type 3 was a paired classification, not the total change between detector settings or an additive causal component. Trial simulations should evaluate eligibility and measurement together; effects on randomized treatment contrasts and power were not assessed.
Keywords: natural history; seizure variability; measurement error; eligibility; digital biomarker; placebo response

Regression to the mean (RTM) is a general threat to clinical-trial interpretation when participants are selected during unusually high baseline values and outcomes are defined as change from that baseline. The design is common in disorders with fluctuating symptoms or events, where apparent improvement may occur even without treatment

 Objective
 A realistic seizure diary simulator is currently unavailable for many research needs, including clinical trial analysis and evaluation of seizure detection and seizure‐forecasting tools. In recent years, important statistical features of seizure diaries have been characterized. These include (1) heterogeneity of individual seizure frequencies, (2) the relation between average seizure rate and standard deviation, (3) multiple risk cycles, (4) seizure clusters, and (5) limitations on inter‐seizure intervals. The present study unifies these features into a single model.
 
 
 Methods
 Our approach, Cyclic Heterogeneous Overdispersed Clustered Open‐source L‐relationship Adjustable Temporally limited E‐diary Simulator (CHOCOLATES) is based on a hierarchical model centered on a gamma Poisson generator with several modifiers. This model accounts for the aforementioned statistical properties. The model was validated by simulating 10 000 randomized clinical trials (RCTs) of medication to compare with 23 historical RCTs. Metrics of 50% responder rate (RR50) and median percent change (MPC) were evaluated. We also used CHOCOLATES as input to a seizure‐forecasting tool to test the flexibility of the model. We examined the area under the receiver‐operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) for test data with and without cycles and clusters.
 
 
 Results
 The model recapitulated typical findings in 23 historical RCTs without the necessity of introducing an additional “placebo effect.” The model produced the following RR50 values: placebo: 17 ± 4%; drug 38 ± 5%; and the following MPC values: placebo: 13 ± 6%; drug 40 ± 4%. These values are similar to historical data: for RR50: placebo, 21 ± 10%, drug: 43 ± 13%; and for MPC: placebo: 17 ± 10%, drug: 41 ± 11%. The seizure forecasts achieved an AUC of 0.68 with cycles and clusters, whereas without them the AUC was 0.51.
 
 
 Significance
 CHOCOLATES represents the most realistic seizure occurrence simulator to date, based on observations from thousands of patients in different contexts. Design simulations should vary the entry threshold, baseline duration, within-person variability, sensitivity, false alarms, missingness and correction rules. Protocols should state how these enter eligibility and endpoint calculations. Comparisons should distinguish a common potential population with condition-specific enrollment from fixed enrolled membership and fixed trial windows. Paired classifications require a stated truth model and compatible reference scales. Reduced observed RTM alone does not demonstrate greater trial efficiency.

The numerical estimates are specific to the seizure-diary model, rolling selection design, internal finite-history reference and correction rules. They should not be transported directly to another study or disease. The definitions can be applied to other fluctuating outcomes, but measurement-only Type 3 requires paired measured and true-count classifications, or an explicitly justified reference standard. Direct numerical comparison with a fixed-baseline study or a study using a separate long-term diary would mix designs.

The common underlying population and reproducible seeds allow controlled changes to simulation inputs. Several limitations remain. CHOCOLATES is synthetic and its empirical calibration diaries may contain reporting errors, so treating generated counts as biological truth is an idealization. The transient replacement was not a data-derived illness model. Detector performance was constant across people and time; daily sampling cannot address within-day cycles or time-dependent errors. The 36-month reference is finite and includes the trial window. Monthly flooring can raise expected corrected counts above the sensitivity-scaled true reference. Flooring and the rounded daily interval correction can affect selection and classification. Type 3 depends on these modeling choices and is not a separate biological cause. Fixed-enrollment comparisons do not provide an additive causal decomposition. The analysis assessed within-arm apparent improvement, not bias in a randomized treatment contrast, statistical power or optimal trial efficiency.

Transient rate changes, eligibility selection and detector errors can alter apparent improvement in simulated epilepsy trials without treatment. Measurement-only Type 3 RTM occurs when measured counts meet the RTM criterion and true counts do not for the same selected participant and window. Joint simulation of eligibility and measurement can distinguish this category from overall observed RTM while preserving the limits of within-arm inference.
